mcqs.question: Why can SAST analyze code paths that are rarely exercised by any test suite, something DAST cannot do?
options: SAST is always faster to run than any test suite
SAST automatically generates new test cases for every untested branch
SAST only works on code paths that have 100% test coverage already
SAST analyzes the source code directly without executing it, so it can inspect every line and branch regardless of whether any test or request actually triggers that path
mcqs.explanation: Because SAST never runs the program, it isn't limited to paths that get exercised at runtime — it can inspect every branch statically, which is exactly the coverage advantage DAST (which requires actually triggering behavior) doesn't share. SAST speed varies by tool and codebase size, it doesn't generate test cases, and it specifically doesn't require any existing test coverage to analyze a path.

mcqs.question: A DAST scan finds no vulnerabilities in a web application's exposed endpoints. Can this scan detect a bug hidden in an admin feature that's disabled by a feature flag and never reachable through the tested surface?
options: Yes, because DAST inspects the underlying source code regardless of what's reachable
No — DAST can only test what it can actually reach and exercise through the running application's exposed surface; a code path never reachable during the scan goes untested
Yes, because DAST automatically enables every feature flag before scanning
No, because DAST cannot test any web application regardless of configuration
mcqs.explanation: DAST's coverage is bounded by what it can actually trigger from outside — a disabled or hidden feature path it never reaches simply isn't tested, which is a real and structural limitation of black-box testing. DAST doesn't read source code at all, doesn't automatically flip feature flags, and is fully capable of testing reachable web application surfaces.

mcqs.question: What makes coverage-guided fuzzing (like AFL or libFuzzer) more effective than purely random input generation at finding deep bugs?
options: It only tests inputs that are already known to be safe
It requires the source code to have zero existing bugs before it can run
It instruments the code to see which branches an input exercised, then mutates inputs specifically to explore new code paths rather than retrying already-familiar ones
It replaces the need for any code review or static analysis entirely
mcqs.explanation: Coverage feedback lets the fuzzer target genuinely unexplored code paths instead of wasting cycles re-testing paths already well-covered, which is exactly why it finds rare, deeply-nested bugs far more efficiently than blind random generation. It isn't restricted to known-safe inputs, doesn't require bug-free code to run, and doesn't replace other testing techniques that catch different bug classes.

mcqs.question: Why is fuzzing typically run as a continuous background process rather than as a per-commit CI gate, unlike SAST?
options: Fuzzing requires sustained runtime to explore enough input space to find a bug, which doesn't fit the fast turnaround a per-commit gate needs
Fuzzing is technically incompatible with any CI/CD system
Fuzzing only works on code written in Python
Fuzzing produces no useful output unless run on a live, publicly deployed instance
mcqs.explanation: Fuzzing's value comes from accumulated exploration time — it needs to run for a long stretch to have a realistic chance of hitting a rare crash-inducing input, which is fundamentally at odds with blocking a fast per-commit merge gate. It's not incompatible with CI/CD generally, isn't limited to any one language, and doesn't require a live public deployment to run against.

mcqs.question: A typical CRUD web application with no memory-unsafe code and no untrusted binary parsing is evaluating where to invest limited security testing effort. Why would fuzzing likely deliver less value there than SAST and DAST?
options: Fuzzing is technically impossible to run against web applications
The vulnerability classes fuzzing is best at finding (memory corruption, parser bugs) have little surface to exercise in a codebase without memory-unsafe code or complex untrusted-input parsing
SAST and DAST are always superior to fuzzing for every kind of system
Fuzzing only produces false positives and never finds real bugs
mcqs.explanation: Matching a technique to a system's actual risk profile matters — fuzzing's strengths (memory-safety and parser bugs) are largely absent from a typical CRUD app's surface, so the same effort spent there yields far less than it would against a component that parses untrusted binary input. Fuzzing can run against web applications in principle, SAST/DAST aren't universally superior (each system profile differs), and fuzzing does find real, often serious bugs where its target vulnerability classes exist.

mcqs.question: A team's SAST scan runs clean with zero findings, and they conclude the application has no security vulnerabilities. What's the flaw in that conclusion?
options: A clean SAST result only means no pattern the tool was configured to recognize was found in the source code — it says nothing about business-logic flaws, deployment misconfigurations, or vulnerability classes the tool isn't designed to detect
SAST scans are never accurate and should be ignored entirely
The conclusion is correct, since SAST is a comprehensive guarantee of security when it finds nothing
A clean SAST scan means the application has also passed an equivalent DAST scan automatically
mcqs.explanation: A clean result is evidence of the absence of what that specific tool checks for, not evidence of the absence of vulnerabilities generally — business logic flaws and deployment-time issues are entirely outside SAST's static, source-only view. SAST is genuinely useful despite this limitation, a clean scan is not a comprehensive guarantee, and it has no bearing on whether a separate DAST scan would also pass.
